articles.title: Zoraxy deployments need route-level authentication, not just a hidden admin page
articles.excerpt: Zoraxy deployments need route-level authentication, not just a hidden admin page Zoraxy is a general-purpose HTTP reverse proxy with a web management interface and per-route access options. The useful…
articles.body: Zoraxy deployments need route-level authentication, not just a hidden admin page Zoraxy is a general-purpose HTTP reverse proxy with a web management interface and per-route access options. The useful security question is not whether the management page is hard to guess. It is whether every proxied hostname, alias and path reaches a backend through an intended authentication decision. The project documentation describes basic authentication, forward authentication, OAuth2 and ZorxAuth as available authentication methods. It also documents a no-auth mode for deployments that already have permission management in an upstream proxy. The README warns that no-auth should be used only in a trusted environment or behind another authentication proxy.

articles.title: Time Complexity and Big O Notation: How to Measure Algorithm Speed
articles.excerpt: Stop guessing whether your code is fast — learn to measure it properly. When two programmers debate whose solution is better, the argument often devolves into: "Mine ran in 0.3 seconds." But that's me…
articles.body: Stop guessing whether your code is fast — learn to measure it properly. The Problem with "It Runs Fast on My Machine" When two programmers debate whose solution is better, the argument often devolves into: "Mine ran in 0.3 seconds." But that's meaningless. Your colleague might have a faster CPU. The input might be small. The test might have been run under special conditions. We need a universal, hardware-independent way to describe how fast an algorithm is. That's where time complexity and Big O notation come in. What Is Time Complexity? Time complexity describes how the runtime of an algorithm grows as the size of the input grows. We don't measure actual seconds. We count the number of basic operations — comparisons, assignments, additions — in terms of the input size n .

articles.title: Your GitHub Project Needs a Better Resume Description Than a Tech Stack
articles.excerpt: You spent three weekends building an app. The repository has a working demo, a reasonable README, and more commits than you want to count. On your resume, it becomes one line: “Built a full-stack appl…
articles.body: You spent three weekends building an app. The repository has a working demo, a reasonable README, and more commits than you want to count. On your resume, it becomes one line: “Built a full-stack application using React, Node.js, PostgreSQL, and Docker.” That line names the tools. It leaves out almost everything that would help someone understand your work. A project description should give a reader enough context to decide whether to open the repository. What did the application do? Which parts did you own? What engineering decision can you explain without looking at your notes? You don’t need a popular repository to answer those questions. You need a specific account of your contribution.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.

articles.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
articles.excerpt: Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.
articles.body: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky.

articles.title: I finally got my hands on the Unistellar Envision smart binoculars with augmented reality and I can’t wait to stargaze with them
articles.excerpt: The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.
articles.body: I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek . He was, of course, referencing the red augmented reality (AR) overlay in the Envisions that can identify night sky targets and landmarks, as well as displaying navigational tools. These are the first pair of smart binoculars that can identify targets in the night sky, such as planets, stars and deep space objects. The build is solid and while they aren't the most lightweight binoculars , the body is hiding that extra technology that enables the AR overlay in the right hand lens.

articles.body: Straight from its inspiring live performance at New York City's Carnegie Hall this past April, RadicalMedia's filmed presentation of the immersive living space documentary, "We Chose to Go to the Moon," is finally available for the rest of us to watch. "We Chose to Go to the Moon" premieres Nov. 10 at 8:00 p.m. ET on PBS, PBS.org, and the PBS app, and we’ve got an exclusive clip to share featuring Mark and Kali Armstrong singing "Flight of Fancy." With a poignant introduction by Oscar winning director Ron Howard ("Apollo 13"), "We Chose to Go to the Moon" recalls the extraordinary saga of the global space race and Apollo moon landings by actors portraying pivotal persons who made it all happen.
